summary: Thierry Moreau, OctoAI co-founder, opens by polling the audience, noting the AI Engineer conference crowd has unusually high fine-tuning familiarity. He frames two GenAI pains: costs going through the roof and POCs not meeting production quality bars. The talk covers when to fine-tune, situating it in a crawl-walk-run quality optimization journey (prompt engineering → RAG → fine-tuning), and walking through a full continuous deployment cycle: dataset collection, fine-tuning, deployment, and evaluation. Fine-tuning criteria include specific tasks, high-quality data, and economic incentive; the cycle is iterative due to production data drift. For datasets, Moreau describes a spectrum from real-world human prompts and responses (highest quality), to real-world prompts with AI-generated responses (enabled by OpenPipe logging), to fully synthetic data (good for starting). He stresses train/validation/test splits and starting with smaller open-source models like Llama 3 8B, citing weight ownership and deployment flexibility as key advantages. Fine-tuning techniques include LoRA (~50 MB, multiple fine-tunes per GPU, sufficient for specialized tasks) and full-parameter checkpoints (~15 GB, for complex reasoning). Fine-tuning can be DIY (Axol) or SaaS (OpenPipe, lowering barriers). Deployment options range from DIY (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, TGI) to SaaS via OctoAI, which offers ~150 tokens/sec at $0.15/million tokens vs $30 for GPT-4, serving 20+ billion tokens/day. OctoStack addresses on-prem/VPC needs. Evaluation splits into automated pass/fail tests and soft evaluations requiring human judgment or LLM-as-judge, with cautions about self-favoring bias. The practical demo uses PII redaction via function calling with the ai4privacy Pi-masking 200k dataset (54 PII classes, 229 discussion subjects). Moreau builds a 10,000-sample training dataset formatted as logged LLM messages, uploads to OpenPipe (90/10 train/test split), and launches a LoRA fine-tune on Llama 3 8B with 32k context (Theta variant from Nous Research), costing ~$40. The fine-tune produces a 50 MB LoRA adapter exported as fp16 and uploaded to OctoAI's asset library for deployment, though the live upload fails and he falls back to a pre-uploaded asset. Quality evaluation uses an accuracy metric with ground-truth labels, penalizing false positives and false negatives, with a similarity distance metric for near-matches. On 100 test samples, the fine-tuned model achieves 0.97 accuracy vs GPT-4's 0.68. Moreau concludes that fine-tuning is a rewarding but never-ending journey requiring continuous monitoring. He closes by inviting questions, offering $10 in OctoAI credits for completing a short survey, directing attendees to the booth, and encouraging them to try the notebook once the LoRA upload issue is fixed.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Fine-tuning is not a silver bullet—try prompt engineering and RAG first before committing to fine-tuning
Fine-tuning is best suited for highly specific, focused tasks such as classification, information extraction, and function calling
High-quality proprietary data is essential; a model is only as good as its training data, ideally matching real-world production data
Start with smaller open-source models like Llama 3 8B; scale up only if results are insufficient
LoRA (~50MB) is sufficient for specialized tasks like function calling; full-parameter checkpoints (~15GB) suit complex reasoning
Open-source fine-tuning grants ownership of model weights and deployment flexibility, avoiding vendor lock-in
OctoAI delivers ~150 tokens/sec at $0.15/million tokens vs $30 for GPT-4, serving 20+ billion tokens/day
Function calling as a fine-tuning target provides output flexibility (masking, anonymization, substitution) beyond simple text redaction
OpenPipe handles hyperparameters automatically and lowers the barrier to fine-tuning as a SaaS solution

sections.title: Introduction and Audience Engagement
sections.summary: Moreau welcomes the audience, polls familiarity with fine-tuning, and notes the AI Engineer conference crowd has unusually high hands-on experience compared to typical audiences.

sections.title: Problem Context and Talk Overview
sections.summary: Two GenAI pains are introduced: soaring costs and POCs not meeting production quality. The talk will cover why and when to fine-tune, the crawl-walk-run framework, and a continuous deployment cycle. The use case is PII redaction.

sections.title: Tools and Results Preview
sections.summary: OpenPipe is introduced as a SaaS fine-tuning solution requiring no hardware, and OctoAI for production deployment. Previewed results: 47% accuracy improvement and 99.5% cost reduction (200x) from GPT-4 Turbo to Llama 3.

sections.title: Crawl-Walk-Run Quality Optimization Framework
sections.summary: Moreau maps quality optimization to crawl (prompt engineering: specificity, few-shot, chain of thought), walk (RAG: complementing parametric memory with non-parametric context), and run (fine-tuning: for highly specific tasks with high-quality proprietary data).

sections.title: When to Fine-Tune and Continuous Deployment Cycle
sections.summary: Fine-tuning criteria: specific tasks, high-quality data, economic incentive. The continuous deployment cycle (dataset building, fine-tuning, deployment, evaluation) is iterative due to data drift. Step one—building the fine-tuning dataset—is introduced.

sections.title: Dataset Building Strategies
sections.summary: Moreau describes a spectrum of dataset sources: real-world human prompts and responses (highest quality), real-world prompts with AI-generated responses (good middle ground, enabled by OpenPipe logging), and fully synthetic data (great for getting started). He emphasizes splitting data into training, validation, and test sets.

sections.title: Model Selection: Open Source vs Closed Source, Small vs Large
sections.summary: Moreau advocates for open-source models, citing weight ownership and deployment flexibility. He recommends starting with smaller models like Llama 3 8B or Mistral 7B, scaling up only if results are insufficient.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning Techniques: LoRA vs Checkpoints and DIY vs SaaS
sections.summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, ~50MB) is contrasted with full-parameter checkpoints (~15GB). LoRA enables serving multiple fine-tunes per GPU and suffices for specialized tasks. DIY tools like Axol offer control; SaaS like OpenPipe lowers barriers.

sections.title: Deployment Options and OctoAI Advantages
sections.summary: Deployment options span DIY (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face TGI) or SaaS via OctoAI. OctoAI offers ~150 tokens/sec, $0.15/million tokens vs $30 for GPT-4, no customization tax, and serves 20+ billion tokens/day. OctoStack addresses on-prem/VPC needs.

sections.title: Quality Evaluation Techniques
sections.summary: Evaluation splits into automated pass/fail tests (code execution, JSON formatting, classification accuracy) and soft evaluations requiring human judgment or LLM-as-judge. Moreau cautions about self-favoring bias when using GPT-4 to evaluate against GPT-4 outputs.

sections.title: Demo Transition and PII Redaction Use Case Context
sections.summary: Moreau transitions to the practical demo, pointing to a QR code and Slack channel for the Colab notebook. He introduces the PII redaction use case using the ai4privacy Pi-masking 200k dataset with 54 PII classes across 229 discussion subjects, including customer tickets, banker conversations, and personal exchanges. The approach uses function calling rather than text generation for redaction output, providing flexibility to mask, anonymize, or substitute PII with fake entries from a mapping database.

sections.title: Building the Fine-Tuning Dataset in Colab
sections.summary: Moreau demonstrates building the dataset in the Colab notebook. Prerequisites include OctoAI and OpenPipe accounts plus an OpenAI key for evaluation. He loads the Pi-masking dataset from Hugging Face, defines a system prompt describing 56 PII categories in natural language, and creates a tool specification as a JSON dictionary with PII types as enums. Each training sample is formatted as logged LLM messages (system prompt, tool spec, user prompt, expected tool-call response), producing 10,000 training samples exported as a JSONL file.

sections.title: Uploading to OpenPipe and Launching the Fine-Tune
sections.summary: Moreau uploads the JSONL dataset to OpenPipe, creating a dataset named 'lunch and learn June 26.' OpenPipe handles preprocessing including a 90/10 train/test split. From the dataset UI, he launches a fine-tune on a Llama 3 8B model with 32k context (Theta variant from Nous Research), with an estimated training cost of $40. New OpenPipe users receive $100 credit. Training produces a LoRA adapter and sends an email when complete. Moreau uses a pre-prepared model to avoid waiting, and notes deployment will use OctoAI.

sections.title: OpenPipe Model UI and Fine-Tuned Model Overview
sections.summary: Moreau shows the OpenPipe model UI, browsing training samples with input columns (system prompt, user prompt, tool choice, tool specification) and output columns (tool-call response with redact arguments as list of dictionaries containing string and PII type). He reviews the fine-tuned Llama 3 8B model trained on 9,000 samples with 1,000 test samples, noting OpenPipe automatically handles hyperparameters like learning rate and number of epochs.

sections.title: Exporting LoRA Weights and Uploading to OctoAI
sections.summary: Moreau exports the fine-tuned model as an fp16 LoRA (~50 MB) from OpenPipe, copying a download URL. He installs the OctoAI CLI to upload the LoRA to OctoAI's asset library, which stores custom checkpoints and LoRAs for serving. After logging in and validating credentials, he attempts to create an asset from the LoRA URL, but the upload step fails during the live demo. He falls back to a previously uploaded LoRA asset to continue the demonstration.

sections.title: Running Inference on the Deployed Fine-Tuned Model
sections.summary: Moreau runs an example inference on the deployed fine-tuned model via an OctoAI endpoint using the standard OpenAI chat completions API, passing the OpenPipe Llama 3 8B 32k model name and the LoRA asset name. The response correctly contains tool calls with the redaction function, confirming the model behaves as intended.

sections.title: Quality Evaluation: Fine-Tuned Model vs GPT-4
sections.summary: Moreau runs quality evaluation on 100 test samples using an accuracy metric with ground-truth labels from the dataset, penalizing false positives and false negatives, with a similarity distance metric for near-matches. The fine-tuned model achieves 0.97 accuracy vs GPT-4's 0.68. Individual examples show the fine-tune correctly identifying PII that GPT-4 misses. Running 100 samples with GPT-4 cost about $1 in inference.

sections.title: Conclusions and Calls to Action
sections.summary: Moreau concludes that fine-tuning is a rewarding but never-ending journey requiring continuous monitoring and retuning. He reiterates the 200x cost difference ($30/million tokens for GPT-4 vs $0.15 for Llama 3 on OctoAI). He directs attendees to octo.cloud, the G7 booth, and a Slack channel, and gives a shout-out to colleague Pedro for a talk on OctoAI's compiler and systems optimization background enabling efficient inference at positive margins.

sections.title: Closing Remarks, Survey Credits, and Q&A Invitation
sections.summary: Moreau closes by inviting questions and announcing that filling out Pedro's survey earns an additional $10 in OctoAI credits, noting that at $0.15 per million tokens this represents a large amount of free generation. He offers to answer questions at the booth and after the talk, thanks the audience, hopes he has demystified fine-tuning, and encourages attendees to try the Colab notebook once the LoRA upload issue is resolved.
